bib.title: Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models

question: Can a two-stage prompt (decompose a problem into easier subproblems, then solve them in sequence) let language models solve problems harder than the exemplars in the prompt, where chain-of-thought prompting fails?
hypothesis: Decomposing into subproblems and feeding earlier answers into later ones gives easy-to-hard generalization that chain-of-thought lacks.
contributions: Least-to-most prompting: few-shot decomposition stage then sequential subproblem solving, no training or finetuning
Results on last-letter concatenation, SCAN (any split, incl. length) and GSM8K/DROP
Prompts for all tasks in the Appendix

method.summary: Few-shot prompting of GPT-3 code-davinci-002 (also text-davinci-002, code-davinci-001, a 540B LM) in two stages: a decomposition prompt lists subproblems, then a solving prompt answers them in order, each prompt appending earlier sub-answers. Compared against standard few-shot and chain-of-thought prompts built from the same exemplars. No training.
method.task: easy-to-hard generalization: symbolic manipulation, compositional generalization (SCAN), math/numerical reasoning (GSM8K, DROP)

datasets.name: GSM8K

datasets.name: DROP (numerical subset)
datasets.size: code-davinci-002 sizes not stated; text-davinci-002: 500 non-football + 500 football random; LM-540B: 3988 non-football + 1862 football

models.name: code-davinci-002 (GPT-3)
models.context: inferred: input limit usually up to 2048 tokens (text: language models usually up to 2048 tokens)

inference.samples: single run per setting; no seeds, repeats or confidence intervals stated
inference.prompting: Last-letter: 2 exemplars (LtM decomposition 1 exemplar; solution 2 base+recursive exemplars; also 4- and 8-shot variants). SCAN: decomposition prompt 8 exemplars, mapping prompt 14 exemplars. GSM8K: 1-shot merged prompt (Table 9) or best: decomposition 7 + solving 4 examples. DROP: non-football decomposition 5 + solving 3; football decomposition 6 + solving 3; CoT and standard 3 examples; zero-shot format 'Q: {question} A: The answer is'.

parameters.stages: 2 (decomposition, then sequential solving); stages can be merged for GSM8K
parameters.GSM8K 1-shot: prompt ends 'Let's break down this problem:', then a second request appends 'The answer is:'

other.full_prompts: Full prompt contexts: SCAN App 8.1 (pp.29-31), DROP App 9 (pp.46-51), GSM8K App 10.3-10.4 (pp.57-61)

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: exact-match of final answer (SCAN action sequence after expanding Python expressions; last-letter string; numeric answer for GSM8K/DROP after postprocessing)

baselines: CoT original 8-shot of Wei et al. 2022 (GSM8K)
eval.protocol: Single evaluation per cell; no significance tests; answer extraction by postprocessing; error analyses on 20 random failures per setting.

prompts.text:
Q: “think, machine, learning”
A: “think”, “think, machine”, “think, machine, learning”

prompts.purpose: Last-letter solution, base case + recursive step (Table 2)
prompts.text:
Q: “think, machine”
A: The last letter of “think” is “k”. The last letter of “machine” is “e”. Concatenating “k”, “e” leads to “ke”. So, “think, machine” outputs “ke”.
Q: “think, machine, learning”
A: “think, machine” outputs “ke”. The last letter of “learning” is “g”. Concatenating “ke”, “g” leads to “keg”. So, “think, machine, learning” outputs “keg”.

Q: Elsa has 5 apples. Anna has 2 more apples than Elsa. How many apples do they have together?
A: Let’s break down this problem: 1. How many apples does Anna have? 2. How many apples do they have together?
1. Anna has 2 more apples than Elsa. So Anna has 2 + 5 = 7 apples.
2. Elsa and Anna have 5 + 7 = 12 apples together.
The answer is: 12.
prompts.where: Table 9; App 10.3.2 has a slightly different wording

prompts.text:
Q: “look opposite right thrice after walk”
A: “look opposite right thrice” can be solved by: “look opposite right”, “look opposite right thrice”. “walk” can be solved by “walk”. So, “look opposite right thrice after walk” can be solved by: “look opposite right”, “look opposite right thrice”, “walk”.

limits: Decomposition prompts do not generalize across domains: a math decomposition prompt (Table 9) is not effective for commonsense questions such as 'Did Aristotle use a laptop?' (Sec 5).
Generalizing decomposition is hard even within a domain: nearly all GSM8K problems are solved given the correct decomposition (Sec 5).
Strong results on last-letter and SCAN are attributed to decomposition being straightforward there (Sec 5).
On GSM8K the overall gain is small (60.87 to 62.39) and nil with engineered prompts (68.01 vs 68.613); the gain is concentrated in problems with at least 5 steps.
Model-dependent: code-davinci-002 beats text-davinci-002, code-davinci-001 is far worse; no open models, no decoding settings or seeds stated; single run, no intervals.
Model sizes of the GPT-3 variants not stated; DROP test size for code-davinci-002 not stated.
Authors note prompting may not be the best way to teach reasoning (Sec 6).
